Protagonist, antagonist, and anti-hero as structural roles; supporting and minor characters

The actor–character relationship: performance as a component of character
The difference between a character and a star persona

claims.claim: A character in film or television is built across a whole work from multiple components — scripted dialogue and action, performance, costume and appearance, casting, and editing choices — rather than being delivered fully in one scene.

Performance is a component of character: actors' faces, bodies, delivery, gesture, and timing are observable material, and screen performance styles have evolved with cinematic language rather than staying fixed.
Costume, hair, and make-up are designed to fit the character, the setting, and the story, and they help actors inhabit their roles.

The protagonist is the central character whose pursuit, choices, or situation drives the story; the antagonist's structural role is to oppose or block the protagonist's progress; an anti-hero is a flawed or unsympathetic central figure distinct from the antagonist.

Round characters are complex, often internally conflicted, and usually change over the course of a story; flat characters lack that complexity, do not change, and typically exist to support the central characters.
Editing shapes the character viewers see: the editor selects among takes and orders shots, so the on-screen performance is partly constructed in post-production.

A star persona — the public image and celebrity associations built by the star system — is distinct from any single character; audiences may see the star as much as the character, and formal analysis should keep the two layers separate.

Character development or change should be described from evidence: compare behavior early and late in a work, identify the events the work links to the change, and avoid quality judgments without shown support.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Popular discourse often treats an actor's fame and the character they play as interchangeable, while formal analysis treats them as separate layers.
positions: Casting and marketing deliberately foreground stars so audiences follow them across roles (Moving Pictures acting chapter).
Formal analysis keeps the work-built character distinct from the performer's public image so each can be described on its own evidence.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents character and star persona as separate layers that interact, and instructs analysis to describe each on its own evidence before noting the interaction.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft described 'character' as a generic toolbox-label concept with no film-specific content; that framing was discarded as boilerplate.
The draft's generic objectives, vocabulary, and questions did not test any film-character concepts and were replaced entirely.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the machine-generated boilerplate lesson with a film-specific formal-analysis lesson.
Added source verification for all character concepts using the Moving Pictures chapters (Acting, Narrative, Mise-en-Scène, Introduction) and the MIT OpenCourseWare viewing handout.
Replaced the draft questions with five sourced questions covering roles, round/flat characters, formal layers, character change, and star persona.
All examples were rewritten as original invented scenes to avoid reproducing any film dialogue, clips, or stills.
rightsIssues: None identified: all sources are CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 open textbooks or an official MIT OpenCourseWare handout used as reference; the lesson reproduces no source prose, film dialogue, clips, screenshots, or stills.

The lesson uses original synthesis only; embedded third-party video links were not reproduced.
